question: As the CEO, compare voluntary attrition, employee engagement, and workforce cost across Engineering and Sales. Explain what the combination suggests, what it cannot prove, and recommend three practical actions.
title: Prioritize Sales retention diagnosis and Engineering cost discipline—not blanket interventions
answer: Sales & marketing has higher voluntary attrition than Engineering despite almost identical employee favorability. Engineering carries the larger workforce cost and absolute over-plan amount. This supports different management priorities, but does not establish that engagement or pay causes turnover, or that Engineering is less efficient.

evidence.definition: Voluntary exits / mean FTE, annualized; short windows are not forecasts.
Favorable survey responses / respondents, not all employees.
Annual loaded workforce run rate minus comparable annual plan; not booked savings.

followups: Compare monthly attrition, favorability and cost trends to assess whether this quarterly contrast persists.

analysis.summary: Sales & marketing has higher voluntary attrition than Engineering despite almost identical employee favorability. Engineering carries the larger workforce cost and absolute over-plan amount. This supports different management priorities, but does not establish that engagement or pay causes turnover, or that Engineering is less efficient.

sections.title: Attrition differs; reported engagement barely does
sections.text: For July–September 2026, annualized voluntary attrition is 7.0% in Engineering versus 10.0% in Sales & marketing. At September 30, employee favorable responses are 72.0% and 72.1%, respectively, with survey participation of 60.0% in both. The engagement proxy therefore does not visibly distinguish the functions’ different turnover rates.

sections.title: Engineering has the larger spending exposure—and workforce
sections.text: At September 30, Engineering’s annual loaded workforce cost run rate is $420m, versus $180m for Sales & marketing. Engineering is $12m above its comparable annual plan; Sales & marketing is $5m above plan. Employee headcount is 2,400 and 1,200, respectively. These are total spending comparisons, not efficiency measures: cost includes contractors and overtime, while employee headcount excludes contractors.

sections.title: What the combination suggests
sections.text: Sales & marketing merits an investigation of retention risks that an overall engagement score may miss—for example, incentive design, career opportunities, workload or external hiring demand. Engineering merits a review of whether its spending supports valuable delivery capacity. Neither interpretation is established: workforce composition could explain cost differences, and broad survey averages could conceal variation within either function.

sections.title: What this cannot prove
sections.text: The available Sales segment includes marketing; it is not Sales alone. All figures are synthetic. Attrition is annualized from a quarter, not a forecast; engagement is a September snapshot among respondents, not all employees. Equal participation does not eliminate nonresponse bias. Cost is an annual run rate, not quarterly or year-to-date expenditure. These aggregates establish neither causation nor statistical significance, and do not measure compensation competitiveness, lost revenue, delivery productivity or the financial return from retention spending.

sections.title: 1. Run a focused Sales retention diagnostic
sections.text: Ask the CHRO and commercial leader to complete a 30-day review of privacy-safe turnover patterns by tenure, role and region, alongside aggregate exit and stay-interview themes. Test incentive clarity, career progression and workload as competing explanations. Identify whether departures threaten customer coverage before proposing targeted interventions; do not default to an across-the-board pay increase.

sections.title: 2. Reconcile workforce spending to business capacity
sections.text: Have Finance and the functional leaders explain each over-plan amount through staffing, role/location mix, contractors, overtime and compensation. Prioritize Engineering’s larger absolute exposure, but review both functions. Require any hiring or cost-reduction proposal to specify the delivery milestones or customer coverage it protects, its cash implications and its capacity risks—rather than treating lower spend as inherently better.

sections.title: 3. Pilot a targeted response and establish a decision gate
sections.text: After diagnosis, test one specific intervention in comparable teams using a phased rollout or comparison group. Set a 90-day operating review for participation, targeted survey items, implementation quality, cost and business-capacity measures; assess retention over a longer observation window. Scale only if the evidence supports improvement without damaging customer coverage or delivery. Treat early results as provisional, not proven savings.

unknowns: Whether Sales alone follows the combined Sales & marketing pattern.
Which roles and tenure groups drive turnover, and how business-critical those departures are.
The drivers of over-plan spending and the business outputs supported by that spending.
